syllabus.clause: Pin exists because an async state machine may hold references into itself after its first poll, and these break if the value moves. Pin<&mut Self>, Unpin, the pin! macro, and pin projection (pin-project-lite) with structural vs non-structural pinning.

at.step: A self-referential value's own pointer breaks the instant it moves
Pin<Ptr> is a promise about the pointee, enforced by the type
Pinned — on the heap or the stack — the identical self-reference stays valid
A pinned field projects by the type's own choice, not automatically

items.item: a key example of an address-sensitive type is the state machine the compiler generates to implement Future for async fns

items.item: Unpin is automatically implemented for almost every type; the compiler marks a type Unpin so long as every type composing its fields is also Unpin

items.item: the pin_project! macro creates a projection type covering all the fields of a struct, where a #[pin] field projects to Pin<&mut T> and an ordinary field projects to a plain reference

at.step: A pinned field projects by the type's own choice, not automatically

items.item: A self-referential value (one holding a pointer into one of its own fields) is sound only as long as it never moves after that pointer is formed — the moment it moves, mechanically, the pointer still refers to the old address, which is now someone else's memory.

at.step: A self-referential value's own pointer breaks the instant it moves

items.item: The standard library names the compiler's generated async state machines as the canonical example of a self-referential type, which is why this topic can demonstrate the exact mechanism with a hand-written stand-in struct rather than needing to show the hidden enum directly.

at.step: Yes — and the standard library names the exact place this happens by default

items.item: Putting a self-referential value behind an ordinary Box<T> does not fix anything: a Box only guarantees the heap allocation's address is stable, but the T inside it can still be moved out (mem::replace, or an owning move), carrying the same stale-pointer problem with it.

at.step: Does wrapping it in a Box<T> fix this?

items.item: Pin<Ptr> is not a container that holds a value more safely; it is a promise, carried by the type itself, that the pointer's pointee will not move or be invalidated for as long as the Pin exists — a guarantee the type system can check mechanically rather than one left to documentation.

at.step: Pin<Ptr> is a promise about the pointee, enforced by the type

items.item: Unpin is an auto trait: almost every ordinary type gets it for free, and a type that implements Unpin is explicitly saying it never needed Pin's guarantee in the first place, so pinning it has no extra effect at all — PhantomPinned exists specifically to opt a type back out of Unpin.

at.step: Pin<Ptr> is a promise about the pointee, enforced by the type

items.item: Box::pin (heap) and the pin! macro (stack) are two different places to put the exact same promise; a self-reference formed after either one stays valid for the same reason in both cases — nothing in the safe API can move the pinned value out from under it.

at.step: Pinned — on the heap or the stack — the identical self-reference stays valid

items.item: Pin's guarantee is enforced by the compiler, not merely documented: attempting to move a !Unpin value out of a Pin<Box<T>> (or any Pin<Ptr>) fails to compile with a real, specific error, because Pin<Box<T>> only exposes a plain, ownable T through DerefMut when T: Unpin.

at.step: rustc's own diagnostic: this move is rejected outright

items.item: Pin projection is a deliberate, per-field choice made by the author of a type, never automatic: a field can be declared structurally pinned (it moves exactly when its container does, and projects to Pin<&mut Field>) or left unpinned (projects to a plain reference) — getting this choice wrong in hand-written unsafe code is exactly the hazard pin-project-lite's generated code exists to rule out.

at.step: A pinned field projects by the type's own choice, not automatically

items.item: In production, almost no code manually implements Pin projection with unsafe code; crates like pin-project and pin-project-lite exist precisely because getting structural vs non-structural projection right by hand is easy to get wrong and hard to notice when it's wrong, since the mistake only becomes unsound, not a compile error.

at.step: A pinned field projects by the type's own choice, not automatically

items.item: This chapter's whole arc — a future that does nothing until polled, the waker contract, the generated state machine, and now Pin — has been entirely about one future running correctly by itself; nothing so far has required more than one thread to exist at all.

at.step: Recap: self-reference, Pin's promise, and projection, proven both ways
